title: Epitome Divinarum Institutionum
author: Lactantius
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0171.stoa008.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Orpheus principalem deum dicit, qui caelum solemque cum ceteris astris, qui terram, qui maria condiderit.
passages.english: Orpheus speaks of a chief god, who founded the sky and the sun together with the other stars, who [founded] the earth, who [founded] the seas.

passages.original: Sed ueniamus ad philosophos, quorum certior habetur auctoritas quam poetarum. (Plato) monarchian adserit unum deum dicens, a quo sit mundus instructus (et) mirabili ratione perfectus.
passages.english: But let us come to the philosophers, whose authority is held to be more certain than that of the poets. Plato asserts a monarchy, saying that there is one god, by whom the world was arranged and completed with wonderful design.
passages.notes: 'Plato' and 'et' are supplied by the edition in angle brackets. 'Monarchian' is the Greek word for 'single rule', kept by Lactantius.

passages.original: Superest de uatibus dicere. Varro decem Sibyllas fuisse tradit: primam de Persis, secundam Libyssam, tertiam Delphida, quartam Cimmeriam, quintam Erythraeam, sextam Samiam, septimam Cumanam, octauam Hellespontiam, nonam Phrygiam, decimam Tiburtem, cui sit nomen Albunea.
passages.english: It remains to speak about the prophetesses. Varro reports that there were ten Sibyls: the first from the Persians, the second the Libyan, the third the Delphic, the fourth the Cimmerian, the fifth the Erythraean, the sixth the Samian, the seventh the Cumaean, the eighth the Hellespontine, the ninth the Phrygian, the tenth the Tiburtine, whose name is Albunea.

passages.original: hic Epidauri moratus est, Cynosuris, ut Cicero ait, sepultus, cum esset ictu fulminis interemptus. Apollo autem pater eius non dedignatus est alienum gregem pascere, ut acciperet uxorem; et dilectum puerum cum peremisset inprudens, gemitus suos inscripsit in flore.
passages.english: He lived at Epidaurus, and was buried at Cynosura, as Cicero says, after he had been killed by a stroke of lightning. And Apollo his father did not disdain to pasture another man's herd in order to get a wife; and when he had unwittingly killed a beloved boy, he inscribed his laments on a flower.
passages.notes: The subject 'he' is Aesculapius (Asclepius), as the reference to Apollo his father shows. The boy is Hyacinthus.

passages.original: Faula quoque et Flora meretrices erant, quarum altera Herculis fuit scortum, sicut Verrius tradit, altera cum magnas opes corpore quaesiuisset, populum scripsit heredem et ideo in honorem eius ludi Floralia celebrantur.
passages.english: Faula and Flora too were prostitutes. The first of these was the harlot of Hercules, as Verrius reports; the other, when she had acquired great wealth with her body, wrote the people [down] as her heir, and for that reason the games of the Floralia are celebrated in her honour.
passages.notes: Verrius: presumably the grammarian Verrius Flaccus.

passages.original: quodsi sursum oculos suos tollerent ac deum intuerentur, qui eos ad aspectum caeli suique excitauit, numquam se curuos et humiles facerent terrena uenerando. quorum stultitiam Lucretius grauiter incusat dicens: et faciunt animos humiles formidine diuum depressosque premunt ad terram:
passages.english: But if they would raise their eyes upward and look upon God, who roused them to the sight of heaven and of himself, they would never make themselves bent and lowly by venerating earthly things. Their folly Lucretius severely censures, saying: "and they make their minds lowly through fear of the gods, / and press them down, bowed, to the earth."

passages.original: Hi sunt daemones, de quibus poetae saepe in carminibus suis locuntur, quos custodes hominum appellat Hesiodus. ita enim persuaserunt hominibus inlecebris atque fallaciis suis, ut eosdem deos esse crederent.
passages.english: These are the demons of whom the poets often speak in their songs, whom Hesiod calls the guardians of human beings. For by their enticements and deceptions they so persuaded people that they believed these same [beings] to be gods.

passages.original: Gellius in libris Noctium Atticarum sic dicens: quibus non uidetur mundus dei et hominum causa institutus neque res humanae prouidentia gubernari, graui se argumento uti putant, cum ita dicunt: \'si esset prouidentia, nulla essent mala.\' nihil enim minus aiunt prouidentiae congruere quam in eo mundo quem propter homines fecisse dicatur, tantam uim esse aerumnarum et malorum.
passages.english: Gellius, in the books of the Attic Nights, speaking thus: 'Those who think that the world was not established for the sake of God and human beings, and that human affairs are not governed by providence, believe they are using a weighty argument when they say: "If there were providence, there would be no evils." For they say that nothing fits less with providence than that, in that world which it is said to have made for the sake of human beings, there should be so great a mass of hardships and evils.'
passages.notes: The sentence opens without a main verb; it continues a citation introduced earlier.

passages.original: proinde\' inquit \'homines stulti cur non hoc etiam desiderant, ut ueritas sit et non sit mendacium? namque itidem sunt bona et mala, felicitas et inportunitas, uoluptas et dolor. alterum enim ex altero, sicut Plato ait, uerticibus inter se contrariis deligatum: si tuleris unum, abs-
passages.english: 'Accordingly,' he says, 'why do foolish people not also wish for this, that there be truth and no falsehood? For in the same way there are goods and evils, happiness and misfortune, pleasure and pain. For the one is bound to the other, as Plato says, by mutually opposed ends: if you take away one, you take a-
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-word ('abs-', presumably 'abstuleris', 'you will have taken away'). 'Verticibus' (literally 'tops, ends') is rendered 'ends'.

passages.original: sapientia est, ut Cicero definiuit, diuinarum et humanarum rerum scientia. quae definitio si uera est, non cadit in hominem sapientia.
passages.english: Wisdom is, as Cicero defined it, the knowledge of divine and human things. If this definition is true, wisdom does not fall to a human being.

passages.original: de antipodis quoque sine risu nee audiri nec dici potest, adseritur tamen quasi aliquid serium. ut credamus esse homines qui uestigiis nostris habeant aduersa uestigia. tolerabilius Anaxagoras delirauit, qui nigram niuem dixit.
passages.english: About the antipodes, too, nothing can be either heard or said without laughter, and yet it is asserted as though it were something serious, so that we should believe there are people who have their footprints opposite to ours. Anaxagoras raved more tolerably when he said that snow was black.

passages.original: mitto Socraten, cuius est nota sententia. Anaxagoras omnia circumfusa tenebris esse pronuntiat, Empedocles angustas ad inueniendam ueritatem sensuum semitas esse.
passages.english: I pass over Socrates, whose saying is well known. Anaxagoras declares that all things are surrounded by darkness; Empedocles, that the paths of the senses for finding the truth are narrow.

passages.original: quoniam igitur nulla est, (ut) apud Platonem Socrates dicit, humana sapientia, sequamur ergo diuinam deoque gratias agamus, qui eam nobis et reuelauit et tradidit, ac nobis gratulemur, quod ueritatem ac sapientiam caelesti beneficio tenemus, quam tot ingeniis, tot aetatibus requisitam philosophia[m] num- <quam) potuit inuenire.
passages.english: Since, then, there is no human wisdom, as Socrates says in Plato, let us therefore follow the divine, and give thanks to God, who has both revealed and handed it down to us; and let us congratulate ourselves that by heavenly kindness we hold the truth and wisdom which philosophy, though it was sought by so many minds over so many ages, was never able to find.
passages.notes: The edition's supplements (ut) and num<quam> and its deletion philosophia[m] are followed; 'num- <quam)' is a line-break and bracket scanning error.

passages.original: hic est uirtus, hic ratio, hic sermo dei, hic sapientia. hoc opifice, ut Hermes ait, et consiliatore, at Sibylla, [et] praeclaram et mirabilem huius mundi fabricam machinatus est.
passages.english: He is the power, he the reason, he the word of God, he the wisdom. With him as craftsman, as Hermes says, and as counsellor, as the Sibyl [says], [God] devised the splendid and wonderful fabric of this world.
passages.notes: 'at Sibylla' is evidently a corruption of 'ut Sibylla' ('as the Sibyl [says]'); the bracketed [et] is marked as an editorial deletion and is not translated.

passages.original: Sibylla (Erythraea) quoque deum dicit ducem omnium a deo factum, et alia deum dei filium esse noscendum, sicut ea quae in libris posui exempla declarant.
passages.english: The Erythraean Sibyl also says that God, the leader of all, was made by God, and another [Sibyl says] that God the Son of God is to be acknowledged, as the examples I have set out in the books make clear.

passages.original: Consideremus ergo quae ratio fuerit huius tanti tamque inmensi operis fabricandi. fecit deus mundum, sicut Plato existimauit, sed cur fecerit, non ostendit. quia bonus est inquit et inuidens nulli, fecit quae bona sunt. atquin uidemus in rerum natura et bona esse et mala.
passages.english: Let us therefore consider what was the reason for constructing this so great and so immense a work. God made the world, as Plato judged, but why he made it, he does not show. 'Because he is good,' he says, 'and begrudges no one, he made the things that are good.' And yet we see that in the nature of things there are both goods and evils.

passages.original: inmortales esse animas idem Plato adfirmat: sed cur aut quomodo aut quando aut per quem immortalitatem adsequantur aut quod sit omnino tantum illut mysterium, cur ii qui sunt inmortales futuri, prius mortales nascantur, deinde decurso temporalis uitae spatio atque abiectis fragilium corporum exuuiis ad aeternam illam beatitudinem transferantur, non conprehendit.
passages.english: The same Plato affirms that souls are immortal; but why, or how, or when, or through whom they attain immortality, or what at all that great mystery is, why those who are going to be immortal are first born mortal, and then, when the span of temporal life has run its course and the cast-off coverings of fragile bodies have been thrown aside, are carried over to that eternal blessedness, he does not grasp.

passages.original: Plurimis uero argumentis colligi potest aeternas esse animas. Plato ait, quod per se ipsum semper mouetur nec principium motus habet, etiam finem non habere; animum autem hominis per se semper moueri: qui quia sit ad cogitandum mobilis, ad inueniendum sollers, ad percipiendum facilis, ad discendum capax et quia praeterita teneat, praesentia conprehendat, futura prospiciat multarumque rerum et artium scientiam conplectatur, immortalem esse, siquidem nihil habeat in se de terreni ponderis labe concretum.
passages.english: Indeed, it can be inferred by very many arguments that souls are eternal. Plato says that what is always moved by itself and has no beginning of motion also has no end; and that the mind of man is always moved by itself; and that, because it is quick to think, skilful at discovering, ready at perceiving, capable of learning, and because it holds the past, grasps the present, foresees the future, and embraces the knowledge of many things and arts, it is immortal, since it has in itself nothing compounded of the taint of earthly weight.
